extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science, historians, and readers of Tocqueville; policymakers interested in federalism and republican institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpt from Tocqueville's Democracy in America analyzing causes that strengthen or endanger the American Union and the prospects of republican institutions. Discusses economic, social, institutional, and leadership factors that affect durability of the Union and of republican government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosperity as a source of danger to the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: The prosperity of the United States is the source of the most serious dangers that threaten them, since it tends to create in some of the confederate States that over-excitement which accompanies a rapid increase of fortune; and to awaken in others those feelings of envy, mistrust, and regret which usually attend upon the loss of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville argues that rapid increases in wealth and power create passions (envy, mistrust, regret) that can endanger political union; examples include unequal growth among States and a rush to secure territory and fortune. Prosperity alters feelings and interests and thus can weaken the bond of consent that sustains the confederation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union's continuance depends on the continued assent of confederates
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of the present confederation depends entirely on the continued assent of all the confederates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If States withdraw their assent — either by formally seceding or by tacitly eroding federal authority — the Union can dissolve. Tocqueville uses this as a foundational evaluative principle: the Union is sustained by consent, not by eternal inevitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two distinct modes of dissolution: secession vs. gradual weakening
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union may perish in two different ways: one of the confederate States may choose to retire from the compact (secession), or the authority of the Federal Government may be progressively entrenched on by the simultaneous tendency of the united republics to resume their independence (gradual erosion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should consider whether a crisis is acute (leading to overt secession) or chronic (slow atrophy of federal prerogatives). The gradual weakening can produce internal anarchy and paralysis even if formal union remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercommunication and migration foster national assimilation
rubrics_metrics.description: As Americans intermingle they grow in resemblance of each other; differences from climate, origin, and institutions diminish; the post, steamboats, and inland navigation bring populations into contact and spread common manners and opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures of communication (postal routes, steamboat traffic, inland navigation) and internal migration are criteria for increasing national homogeneity and thus for strengthening the sociocultural foundations of the Union. Tocqueville cites postal miles, steamboat launches, and north–south emigration as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and commercial ties strengthen the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: The commercial ties which unite the confederate States are strengthened by the increasing manufactures of the Americans; and the union which began to exist in their opinions gradually forms a part of their habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Growth of inter-state commerce, manufacturing, and shared economic interests creates habitual connections that make political union more natural and resilient. Evaluations should weigh whether economic integration is deepening or fragmenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal power declines as the original emergency wanes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Constitution was promulgated the nation was a prey to anarchy and the federal power soon reached the maximum of its authority; but once the danger was past, the energy and patriotism which had enabled them to brave it disappeared and the Federal Government brought about its own decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville holds that the necessity that consolidated federal power is temporary; in peaceful prosperity people prefer lighter central action. Assessments of federal strength should account for the life-cycle effect: emergency consolidates power; normalization erodes it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders and parties cultivate provincial jealousies to limit federal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The leaders of parties, who live by the passions of the people, began to work the public tendency to independence to their own advantage; they courted the majority by inveighing against the encroachments of the central power, compelling the Government to recede.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political entrepreneurs who exploit local jealousies and democratic sentiment are a mechanism weakening federal institutions. Evaluation should examine rhetoric and party incentives, not only formal constitutional rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: States resist federal control over internal improvements and lands
rubrics_metrics.description: The States were alarmed at a power distinct from their own (the Federal Government) which could dispose of territory and thus acquire patronage; they claimed rights over Indians and lands, and later demanded revenues from land sales be assigned to new western States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicts over 'internal improvements,' treaty-making (e.g., with Indians), western land disposition, and revenue allocation are concrete loci where state jealousy reveals the limits of federal reach. Legislative concessions (e.g., 1832 law transferring much of land-sale revenue) demonstrate bargaining pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary institutions (Bank of the United States) as a tie and a fault line
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bank of the United States is a great monetary tie of the Union — its notes are accepted across the country — but it is the object of great animosity and political conflict, reflecting deeper antipathies to central power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence and contestation of central monetary institutions indicate the degree of economic integration and the political willingness to accept centralized influence. Attacks on the Bank parallel attacks on federal authority and may signal weakening support for national institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tariff controversy and the doctrine of Nullification as tests of federal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The tariff question revealed Union weakness: tariffs intended to protect Northern manufactures provoked Southern complaints and the revival of the doctrine of Nullification, culminating in South Carolina's convention annulling federal tariff laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy conflicts that align with regional economic interests (e.g., protective tariffs) can escalate into constitutional crises. Evaluations should track whether the federal government can enforce uniform policies across regions or is forced to concede de facto in face of state resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential behavior and popularity can both strengthen and weaken institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: General Jackson supported the Union on the tariff with vigor yet belongs to the party desirous of limiting federal power; he panders to majority passions, sometimes yields to them, and increases personal power even as institutional presidential power or federal authority may decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess leadership not only by formal pronouncements but by how presidents respond to majority passions, use vetoes, assert personal authority, and either defend or undercut federal institutions. Personal popularity may mask institutional erosion if a leader defers to majority impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republican institutions have deeper foundations and greater permanence than the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: The dismemberment of the Union might compromise republican institutions temporarily, but a republican form of government seems the natural state of the Americans and has a much deeper foundation; to destroy it all the laws and manners must be changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish the fragility of a particular political arrangement (the Union) from the resilience of republican habits and beliefs (morality, religion, respect for rights). Evaluations of long-term political outcomes should separate constitutional arrangements from social-political culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republicanism rests on popular morality, religion, and respect for vested rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The republic in the United States is the tranquil rule of the majority founded upon the enlightened will of the people; republicans set a high value upon morality, respect religious belief, and acknowledge the existence of rights. The power of the majority is not unlimited; it recognizes barriers of humanity, justice, reason, and vested rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The durability of republican government should be measured by civic virtues and the majority's willingness to respect moral and legal constraints, not merely by electoral procedures. Tocqueville contrasts this ideal with the demagogue's misuse of majority rule.
